clue.text: Italian city not quite maintaining already disagreeable relationship with host

indicators.note: something not quite complete is short of its final part, so the city's name loses its last letter
to maintain is to hold or keep, so the shortened city holds the next piece inside it

blocks.note: Parma is a city in northern Italy
'as it is' means already, in the present state of things

explanation.surface: Someone already on bad terms with an Italian host city, lodging there grudgingly.
explanation.walkthrough: PARMA minus its final A leaves PARM, which wraps around AS IT IS to make PARASITISM.
explanation.definitionFit: Parasitism is the biological arrangement where one organism lives off another, harming the host it depends on.

clue.text: Perfect language

blocks.note: first meaning: to refine or improve, as a verb
second meaning: the tongue spoken in Poland

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as praise for flawless speech, but the two words are separate meanings; the capital P hides the national sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish something is to refine it to perfection, and Polish is the national tongue of Poland.

clue.text: Overseen by teacher, student ultimately poor performer

indicators.note: in a down entry, being overseen by means sitting below, so the teacher's word comes on top
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is taken

blocks.note: a rabbi is a Jewish religious teacher
the last letter of student

explanation.surface: A weak student under a teacher's supervision.
explanation.walkthrough: A rabbit is British sporting slang, especially in cricket and tennis, for a weak or hopeless player.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a rabbit is an unskilled player, typically a tail-end batsman in cricket who scores few runs.

clue.text: Check match works well!

blocks.note: first meaning: literally striking to test that a match produces flame
second meaning: an old British exclamation of surprise

explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike a light!' is a dated Cockney-style exclamation of astonishment, much like 'Well!' or 'Goodness!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Striking a match tests whether it ignites, and the phrase also serves as a mild British exclamation of surprise.

clue.text: Sugar daddy, say, dispensing with capital

indicators.note: the capital here is the initial letter, which is thrown away

blocks.note: to state is to say

explanation.surface: A wealthy older benefactor who stops handing out money.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Tate founded the sugar refiners later called Tate & Lyle, so he is literally a sugar father; his fortune funded the Tate Gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Henry Tate was the Victorian sugar magnate whose company became Tate & Lyle, a jokey founding father of sugar.

clue.text: Soldier handles climbing about right, weakness following

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading upward, so the word runs backwards
about means surrounding, so the turned word goes around what follows
following means coming straight after, so the weakness sits right behind the letter for right

blocks.note: handles is slang for names
R is the standard abbreviation for right
a vice is a moral failing or weakness

explanation.surface: A soldier grips a rope while climbing, with some weakness showing after.
explanation.walkthrough: Handles meaning names is informal usage, as in someone's 'handle' on a radio.
explanation.definitionFit: A serviceman is a member of the armed forces, so any soldier qualifies.

clue.text: Snapper in pot, did you say

indicators.note: asking whether someone said it points to a word heard rather than read

blocks.note: a crock is an earthenware pot

explanation.surface: A fish or turtle being cooked in a pot, queried by a confused listener.
explanation.walkthrough: A snapper sounds like a fish or turtle, but here it is any creature with snapping jaws.
explanation.definitionFit: A croc, short for crocodile, is famous for snapping its powerful jaws shut on prey.

clue.text: Left sore, one of fifty punches!

indicators.note: to punch is to drive into something, so one piece is driven inside the other

blocks.note: a sore patch of skin is inflamed and red
Maine is one of the fifty US states

explanation.surface: A boxer left aching after one of fifty punches thrown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a direction or a boxing hand, but it is the past tense of stay behind.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean stayed behind: if you remained somewhere, you were left there after others went.

clue.text: Super solving!

blocks.note: first meaning: excellent
second meaning: breaking a code or a problem

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a cheer for the solver; cracking is British informal praise as well as the act of decoding.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracking is informal British praise meaning excellent, and to crack a puzzle or code is to work it out.

clue.text: Where litmus paper may be found in red, or a blue

definitions.text: Where litmus paper may be found

blocks.note: Labour, the red party in British politics, shortened
taken as written
taken as written
blue is the colour of Britain's Conservative or Tory party

explanation.surface: Litmus paper turns red or blue, so the colours seem to describe a chemistry test.
explanation.walkthrough: Red and blue look like litmus results but are British party colours: red for Labour, blue for the Conservatives.
explanation.definitionFit: Litmus paper is a standard chemistry testing strip, the sort of supply kept in a science lab.

clue.text: Hit hard, covers ripped off before returning book

indicators.note: a book's covers are its outer parts, so tearing them off removes the first and last letters
returning means going back the way you came, so the letters are read right to left

blocks.note: to hammer is to hit hard

explanation.surface: A book battered so hard its covers come off before being returned.
explanation.walkthrough: HAMMER without its outer letters gives AMME, which turned round is EMMA, the Jane Austen novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma is the 1815 novel by Jane Austen, so it is a book by title.

clue.text: Critical mark in block of flats, perhaps

blocks.note: key means crucial or critical
a signature is a person's identifying mark

explanation.surface: An essential sign found somewhere in an apartment building.
explanation.walkthrough: Flats here are musical symbols; a key signature groups the flats or sharps at the start of a stave.
explanation.definitionFit: In printed music a key signature is a cluster of flat or sharp symbols at the start of each line.

clue.text: Container in heaven, high

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the first word sits within the second

blocks.note: the sky is poetically the heavens
a tin is a metal container

explanation.surface: A storage box up in the heavens, high above.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' looks like it means lofty, matching heaven, but it means smelly, as of meat gone off.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat or game that is high has begun to go off and smells strongly, which is what stinky means.

clue.text: Composition with citrus twist

blocks.note: a lime is a citrus fruit
to rick is to twist or sprain a joint

explanation.surface: A cocktail recipe garnished with a twist of citrus peel.
explanation.walkthrough: A twist of lime sounds like a drink garnish, but twist is the verb meaning sprain.
explanation.definitionFit: A limerick is a short comic five-line verse, so it is a written composition.

clue.text: Solid flanks good in huge rally

indicators.note: to flank is to stand on either side, so the solid's word wraps around the rest
in means placed inside, so the letter for good goes within the word for huge

blocks.note: a cone is a geometric solid
G is the standard abbreviation for good
great means huge

explanation.surface: Solid support on the edges makes a huge political rally a good one.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two insertions here, one nested inside the other: the letter for good goes in first, then the solid wraps the result.
explanation.definitionFit: To rally is to gather together in a crowd, which is what people do when they congregate.

clue.text: Creator strained Job's patience

indicators.note: something strained is pulled out of shape, so these letters are bent into a new order

blocks.note: all twelve letters, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: God, the Creator, testing Job's legendary patience to breaking point.
explanation.walkthrough: Creator suggests God from the Book of Job, but here it is a creative artist: Jacob Epstein was a 20th-century sculptor.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Jacob Epstein was a celebrated sculptor, and any artist who makes original works is a creator.

clue.text: Breach of faith true, lady not to be trusted

indicators.note: something untrustworthy cannot be relied on to stay as presented, so these letters get rearranged

blocks.note: eight letters taken together

explanation.surface: A seemingly faithful lady turns out to be untrustworthy after all.
explanation.definitionFit: Adultery is betraying marriage vows, a breach of the fidelity promised to a spouse.

clue.text: Poisonous, half a dozen law books

blocks.note: six in Roman numerals
a rule is a law
New Testament, a set of biblical books

explanation.surface: Six toxic law books on a shelf.
explanation.definitionFit: Virulent describes something highly toxic or harmful, such as a venom or an aggressive disease.

clue.text: Playground where one might attempt to remove hooks from swings

definitions.text: Playground where one might attempt to remove hooks from swings

blocks.clueFragment: Playground where one might attempt to remove hooks from swings
blocks.note: surface reading: a children's play area, unhooking the swing seats
setter's reading: in golf a hook is a bad curving shot, and practising swings irons it out

explanation.walkthrough: Playground, hooks and swings all evoke a park, but they are golf terms: a practice ground for swinging clubs and curing hooked shots.
explanation.definitionFit: A driving range is a golf practice area where players hit balls to work on their swing and fix faults.

clue.text: Old rhino somewhere in western Africa

blocks.note: first meaning: a former British gold coin; rhino is old slang for money
second meaning: a West African country

explanation.walkthrough: A rhino seems at home in Africa, but rhino is dated British slang for money; the guinea was a coin worth 21 shillings.
explanation.definitionFit: The guinea was an old British coin, so a sum of old money, and Guinea is a nation on Africa's west coast.

clue.text: Oh no, river has consumed weapon

indicators.note: having consumed something means holding it inside, so the river's name surrounds the other word

blocks.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and in Wales
an arm is a weapon, as in firearms

explanation.surface: Alarm at a river swallowing a weapon thrown into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of dismay used when something has gone wrong.

clue.text: After swallowing that's disgusting, is this the best medicine?

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so the first word goes around the exclamation

blocks.note: later means after
an exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: Someone grimacing after taking a nasty medicine, wondering if it is really the best.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the proverb that laughter is the best medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying 'laughter is the best medicine' holds that a good laugh heals better than any drug.

clue.text: Motherly character?

blocks.note: surface reading: a caring, maternal personality
setter's reading: the character who is a mother, from the familiar personification of the natural world

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as maternal temperament; the question mark warns that the character is Mother Nature herself, and the word also means temperament.
explanation.definitionFit: The natural world is personified as Mother Nature, and the word also means someone's essential character or disposition.

clue.text: Military cap held briefly upon head of infantryman

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter is dropped
the head of a word is its first letter
in a down entry, upon means placed on top, so the shortened word sits above

blocks.note: kept means held
first letter of infantryman

explanation.surface: A soldier's cap held briefly over a foot soldier's head.
explanation.definitionFit: A kepi is the flat-topped peaked cap worn by French soldiers and the Foreign Legion.

clue.text: Suit informally with flower clipped at the front

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Exe runs through Devon
the first letter of clipped

explanation.surface: A suit with a flower clipped onto its front lapel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is crossword code for river, and 'suit' is slang for a business executive.
explanation.definitionFit: A suit is slang for a corporate executive, and exec is the casual short form of executive.

clue.text: Enthralling work required, send for artist

blocks.note: to page someone is to summon them, as over a tannoy
J. M. W. Turner, the English painter

explanation.surface: A gripping artwork is needed, so someone sends for the painter.
explanation.definitionFit: A page-turner is a book so gripping the reader cannot stop turning pages.

clue.text: Caught in eye, tiny hairy thing proving elusive

indicators.note: caught in means held inside, so the letters are found within the words that follow

blocks.note: runs across the two words

explanation.surface: A tiny stray hair caught in someone's eye that will not come out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an eyelash in the eye; the hairy thing is the abominable snowman.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeti is a legendary shaggy ape-like creature of the Himalayas that nobody has ever reliably found.

clue.text: Conscious, put on one's thinking cap

blocks.note: first meaning: intentional, done on purpose, an adjective
second meaning: to ponder carefully, a verb

explanation.walkthrough: One word, two parts of speech: an adjective meaning intended, and a verb meaning to ponder, pronounced differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A conscious act is a deliberate one, intended; and to deliberate is to think hard before deciding.
